voiceover: You believe every human being is equal. That the weak deserve protection. That compassion is good. You think that's obvious. It isn't. For most of history, almost no one believed it — might made right, and the strong ruled. In Rome and Greece, strength was worshipped, slavery was normal, and unwanted babies were left outside to die. Then came a poor Galilean who touched lepers, lifted up women and children, blessed the poor — and died a slave's death on a cross. He taught that every person bears the image of God, that the last would be first, that greatness is serving the weakest. His followers rescued abandoned infants, nursed strangers through plagues, built the first hospitals for the poor, and fought to end slavery. Glen Scrivener calls it the air we breathe: equality, compassion, dignity — values so common we forget they had to be born. The historian Tom Holland concludes that human rights and equality aren't facts of nature; they are a Christian inheritance. The world you love — kinder, freer, more equal than any before it — the carpenter they killed still shapes it.
